items.paragraph: Improvisation in jazz is often imagined as pure spontaneity, music invented from nothing in the moment of performance. The reality is closer to the opposite. Improvisers spend years absorbing scales, harmonic patterns, phrases from recordings and the habits of other players, until a large vocabulary is available to them without conscious thought. What happens on stage is the fresh combination of this material in response to the other musicians and the shape of the tune, not creation from a blank page. Far from diminishing the achievement, this explains it: spontaneity of the kind audiences admire is possible only because so much has been prepared that the performer is free to listen and respond.

items.paragraph: Two pictures of moral worth pull in different directions. On one, the person who is honest only by overcoming a strong temptation to lie deserves more credit than the person to whom lying never occurs, since the first has had to do something and the second has merely been lucky in temperament. Each picture captures something. The struggler's effort is admirable as an achievement, but we would not wish our friends to remain strugglers for ever; we hope that effort will eventually turn into ease. Effort, on this view, is the honourable path to virtue rather than its finest form.

items.paragraph: Nostalgia was once treated as a kind of illness, a homesickness that weakened soldiers and emigrants. A more recent view sees it as doing useful work. People tend to become nostalgic when they feel lonely, uncertain or adrift, and the memories they return to are usually of moments shared with others: a family meal, a school trip, a celebration. Recalling such moments reminds a person that they have been valued and connected, and that sense of continuity can steady them in an unsettled present. Nostalgia is not always benign; it can harden into a refusal to accept change, or into a fantasy of a past that never was. But in its ordinary form it seems less a flight from the present than a way of drawing on the past to cope with it.

items.paragraph: Naming a newly described species after a person is an old habit, and some critics now ask whether names honouring patrons, colonial officials or celebrities should be changed. The case for renaming is easy to feel when the honoured figure was cruel. Yet the strongest reason for caution has little to do with the reputations involved. A scientific name is a retrieval key: it links the specimen in a museum drawer to every paper ever written about it. Change the name and that chain is not cut, since the rules keep track of older names, but it is lengthened and made fragile, especially for the many species known only from a single description in an obscure journal. The more promising reform looks forward: choosing descriptive names for new species costs nothing, while renaming old ones carries a real price in scientific record-keeping.

items.paragraph: Public concern about the decline of pollinators has fastened almost entirely on the honeybee, and campaigns urge people to keep hives in gardens and on city rooftops. The pollinators that are genuinely declining are mostly wild: solitary bees, bumblebees, hoverflies and moths, many of which need particular flowers and undisturbed nesting ground. Adding hives can even make matters worse for these species, because dense colonies of honeybees compete with them for the same nectar and pollen. Those who wish to help pollinators would do better to plant varied native flowers and leave patches of ground untidy.

The lesson is that engagement should be built from the material that is to be learned, not borrowed from material beside it.

items.paragraph: It is often said that a gift made anonymously is morally superior to one made publicly, since the anonymous donor cannot be seeking praise and so must be acting from pure generosity. The reasoning confuses evidence with value. Anonymity can be good evidence that a donor is not after recognition, but a public donor is not thereby shown to be after it, and even a donor who enjoys the praise may give for reasons that are mostly good. More importantly, the recipients are fed and housed just the same either way, and a well-publicised gift may persuade others to give, multiplying its effect. There may be cases where anonymity matters, as when publicity would humiliate the person helped. But as a general ranking, the preference for anonymous giving judges a gift by what it reveals about the giver rather than by what it does.

items.paragraph: Arguments over whether schools should group pupils by ability usually proceed as if the choice were between two outcomes: grouping helps able pupils and harms the rest, or mixing helps the rest at some cost to the able. A lower set taught ambitiously and kept open differs more from a lower set treated as a holding pen than either does from a mixed class. Asking whether grouping works is therefore a less useful question than asking what it is used to do.

items.paragraph: Automation in aircraft cockpits has made flying far safer, since the systems handle routine tasks more consistently than tired humans do. items.paragraph: A familiar complaint about recent fiction is that its villains have become too sympathetic: give every tyrant a sad childhood, the critics say, and evil dissolves into misfortune. Where the criticism does land is on stories that use the backstory to settle the moral question, inviting the reader to feel that a painful past cancels the harm done. items.paragraph: Many systems require passwords to contain capital letters, numbers and symbols, and to be changed every few months. The rules are meant to make passwords harder to guess, but they often achieve the opposite. Faced with demands they cannot remember, people adopt predictable patterns: a capital at the start, a number and an exclamation mark at the end, and a digit increased by one at each forced change. Attackers know these patterns well. Others simply write their passwords down or reuse them across sites. A long phrase that is easy for its owner to remember but not linked to them in any obvious way is generally stronger than a short string of mixed symbols, and it does not need to be changed unless there is reason to think it has been exposed.

items.paragraph: Teachers and parents have long worried that the abbreviations of text messaging, the dropped vowels and phonetic shortcuts, would corrode children's spelling. Suppose a school compares its pupils and finds that the heaviest users of such abbreviations are, if anything, slightly better spellers than the rest. It would be tempting to conclude that texting improves spelling, but the finding cannot carry that weight. To abbreviate a word playfully a child must usually know how it is spelled in full, so skill with abbreviations may simply be a sign of a comfort with language that the better spellers already had. What the finding does undermine is the fear itself: if abbreviating were steadily eroding spelling, the heaviest abbreviators should be doing worse, not better. A correlation that cannot prove benefit can still be evidence against harm.
